query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy nanoalloys used at high temperatures, the predominant factor governing both structural and chemical stability is the inherently sluggish atomic diffusion rather than configurational entropy effects. Reduced atomic mobility limits grain boundary segregation and nanoprecipitate evolution, thereby maintaining a stable disordered solid solution.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic high-entropy nanoalloy synthesized to have a uniformly disordered single-phase microstructure with a controlled grain size.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of nanoalloy samples with identical overall compositions (and hence similar configurational entropy) but systematically vary parameters that modulate diffusion kinetics. This can be achieved by (a) thermal annealing protocols adjusted to produce different grain sizes, and/or (b) the incorporation of trace isotopic markers to differentiate and track atomic diffusion rates.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposures relevant to structural applications (e.g., 800–1000°C) under inert or controlled oxidative environments, where diffusion-driven processes are activated.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries and nano-precipitates that form as a result of atomic rearrangements mediated by diffusion.
generation.mechanism: Sluggish atomic diffusion limits the mobility of constituent atoms, thereby reducing the rate of grain boundary segregation and the nucleation/growth of nanoprecipitates. Even though high configurational entropy favors a disordered solid solution, if diffusion is less active, the alloy’s phase remains stable against chemical inhomogeneities and microstructural coarsening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples engineered to have lower effective atomic diffusivity (via finer grain sizes or isotope modifications) will exhibit reduced signs of phase separation, grain boundary segregation, and nanoprecipitate formation over time compared to baseline samples with higher diffusion rates. This translates into better retention of structural integrity and chemical homogeneity under high-temperature operation.
generation.baseline: High-entropy nanoalloy samples produced with standard thermal processing that yield average grain sizes and unmodified diffusion kinetics.
generation.boundary: The prediction applies primarily under high-temperature regimes (approximately 800–1000°C) typical for elevated-temperature applications. At temperatures significantly lower or higher than this range, or under aggressive chemical environments (beyond controlled oxidation), other mechanisms may dominate the stability behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative magnitude of improved stability due to reduced diffusion is uncertain and may depend on specific alloy compositions and processing details. Additionally, secondary effects (such as stress-induced transformations) may interplay with diffusion-driven processes.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two groups of identical composition high-entropy nanoalloy samples. In Group A, introduce processing conditions (e.g., enhanced grain refinement or isotopic tracer techniques) that are known to further slow the effective atomic diffusion. In Group B, process the samples using conventional protocols. Expose both groups to identical high-temperature conditions (e.g., 900°C) for a fixed duration. Utilize in situ high-temperature electron microscopy combined with spectroscopic analysis (e.g., EDS mapping) to monitor the extent of grain boundary segregation and nanoprecipitate formation over time.
measurements: Size and density of any emergent nanoprecipitates
Overall phase homogeneity via diffraction patterns
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Group A (with slowed diffusion) does not exhibit statistically significant reduction in grain boundary segregation and nanoprecipitate formation compared to Group B, or if both groups show comparable microstructural evolution, then the hypothesis that sluggish diffusion is the primary governing mechanism for stability is falsified.

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Abstract Developing affordable and light high-temperature materials alternative to Ni-base superalloys has significantly increased the efforts in designing advanced ferritic superalloys. However, currently developed ferritic superalloys still exhibit low high-temperature strengths, which limits their usage. Here we use a CALPHAD-based high-throughput computational method to design light, strong, and low-cost high-entropy alloys for elevated-temperature applications. Through the high-throughput screening, precipitation-strengthened lightweight high-entropy alloys are discovered from thousands of initial compositions, which exhibit enhanced strengths compared to other counterparts at room and elevated temperatures. The experimental and theoretical understanding of both successful and failed cases in their strengthening mechanisms and order-disorder transitions further improves the accuracy of the thermodynamic database of the discovered alloy system. decision.trend: Early studies in HEAs first explored phase behavior under energetic processing (e.g., ion irradiation) to correlate multiphase microstructures with stability (PMC4999872), which was then complemented by high‐temperature mechanical tests such as tensile and creep studies (PMC5627260, PMC7512559) that began to unravel how atomic diffusion, grain boundary behavior, and precipitate evolution impact mechanical performance. More recent work has addressed chemical stability under high-temperature oxidation environments (PMC10384371), revealing competing roles for diffusion‐mediated segregation and phase transformation. Overall, the progression moved from phenomenological observations of phase stability toward probing specific mechanisms like diffusion kinetics and boundary segregation, yet without decisively isolating the role of configurational entropy versus atomic mobility.
decision.unsolved: The key unresolved issue remains which mechanistic factor predominantly governs the high-temperature structural and chemical stability of nanoalloys—is it primarily the inherently sluggish diffusion (affecting grain boundary segregation and precipitate evolution) or the configurational entropy effect that stabilizes the disordered phase? The interplay between these factors under controlled conditions has not yet been definitively distinguished.
decision.lever: Design and execute an experiment where nanoalloy samples with identical overall composition (and thus similar configurational entropy) are synthesized while systematically varying parameters that affect diffusion kinetics (for instance, by controlling grain size through thermal annealing protocols or introducing trace isotope markers to modulate and track atomic diffusion rates). In situ high-temperature electron microscopy and spectroscopy would then be used to monitor structural and chemical evolution.
decision.why: By holding configurational entropy constant while precisely tuning diffusion-related parameters, this experiment directly tests the hypothesis that sluggish atomic diffusion (affecting grain boundary segregation and nanoprecipitate evolution) governs the stability of high-entropy nanoalloys. This approach leverages the current trend of isolating individual mechanisms and addresses the critical gap in distinguishing kinetic limitations from entropy stabilization effects.
